No fixed maximum period is acceptable in general because the time needed differs by person, but very long or indefinite treatment could amount to life confinement and raises constitutional doubt, so more support measures and periodic judge review are needed.

Applying the rule to people who offended before the 2006 change does not breach non-retroactivity because it depends on current risk, and their trust interest yields to the major public interest in safety.
Because treatment greatly restricts liberty, the person must be able to appear or send counsel to court when treatment is ordered or stopped, with a defender if they cannot speak fully.

In practice treatment is run by the same authority as punishment, in facilities attached to prisons, with uniform management and little detailed law, so it may drift toward punishment and must be clearly separated.

who: People ordered into forced treatment after serving a sex-crime sentence
People who committed sex offenses before July 2006
Patients with mental disorders or cognitive impairments

raw.answer: Several courts asked Taiwan's Constitutional Court whether it is constitutional that anyone on parole who intentionally commits a new crime and gets a prison sentence must automatically have parole revoked and serve the rest of the old sentence. The court held that this automatic rule goes too far where the new sentence is suspended or is 6 months or less and there is no special need to send the person back. In those cases, the rule violates the principle of proportionality and the protection of personal liberty.
raw.held: Article 78(1) of the Criminal Code is unconstitutional insofar as it automatically revokes parole when the new sentence is suspended or 6 months or less in prison and there is no special-prevention need, and it loses effect from the date of the ruling. Until the law is amended, the authorities must decide case by case whether to revoke parole in such cases.

points.text: Personal liberty is protected, and any restriction must be proportionate; revoking parole sends a person back to prison, so it must meet that standard.
Prison and parole both aim to help prisoners return to society; parole is a transition, and revocation is meant for people who prove unsuited to life in society.

The rule serves an important legitimate purpose, returning unsuitable parolees to prison, but whether to revoke should depend on whether the person is still suited to society and has betrayed the purpose of parole.

Where the new offense got a suspended sentence or 6 months or less, the authorities should examine each case for specific reasons, such as danger to society, risk of reoffending and signs of remorse, that call for return to prison.
Automatic revocation without that examination is not necessary to achieve its purpose, so it violates proportionality and the protection of personal liberty to that extent.

who: People on parole who commit a new intentional crime
People given a suspended sentence or 6 months or less for a new crime

raw.answer: Two people whose land was expropriated by the government asked to take it back, but were refused as being past the deadline. They argued the law never required the government to tell former owners how the land was later used. The court held that this gap violates the constitutional protection of property, and the law must be reviewed and fixed within 2 years.
raw.held: Article 219, paragraph 1 of the Land Act is unconstitutional to the extent that it sets the deadline to start running without requiring regular notice or public announcement of how expropriated land is used, and it must be reviewed and amended within 2 years. Until then, unfinished time limits for taking land back are paused.

points.text: Expropriation is the most serious intrusion on property rights, so the state must follow the strictest procedures, both before and at the time of expropriation.

Once expropriation is complete, if the land is not used as planned or by the deadline, the reason for expropriation is gone. The former owner's right to take the land back is an extension of constitutional property protection, and the state keeps some duty to protect it by fair procedure.
Former owners usually cannot easily learn whether the land is no longer needed or unused, so the authority should regularly notify them, or publicly announce if individual notice is not possible.

The Land Act provision starts the time limit one year after compensation is paid and requires no regular notice or announcement, so people cannot get enough information to decide whether to seek return. This is inconsistent with proper administrative procedure and with the property protection in Article 15.

When adding a notice duty, the law should set shorter or longer reasonable time limits depending on whether notice was given, balancing property protection and legal stability. How the two periods fit together is left to the legislature.
Time limits not yet run out are paused as of the ruling, resume once the authority gives notice or announcement, and then follow the new law once it is passed.

who: Municipal and county authorities in charge of expropriated land
Legislators and agencies revising the law
Persons whose land was taken in general expropriation

raw.answer: A man whose wife died in 2010 applied for survivor's pension under the National Pension Act only in January 2012, and was paid only from the month he applied. The Constitutional Court held that, for deaths on or before 29 February 2016, limiting payment to start from the month of application violates the Constitution. Such survivors may now seek back payment for the period not yet barred by the five-year limit.
raw.held: For deaths occurring on or before 29 February 2016, the rule that survivor's pension starts only from the month of application and eligibility is contrary to the proportionality principle and the protection of property and the right to subsistence, and it no longer applies from the date of the ruling. Those survivors may apply for back payment of pension not yet barred by the five-year limitation.

points.text: Social insurance benefit claims have property value and are protected as property; if they touch minimum living needs they are also protected as the right to subsistence, so restrictions face stricter review.

Survivor's pension aims to stabilize survivors' lives, and survivors often lose their support and struggle to meet minimum living needs. So restrictions must serve an important public interest with a substantial link between means and purpose.

The rule means survivors who did not apply in the first eligible month lose pension for the months before they applied, even if not time-barred, which restricts their claim. A later amendment fixed this only for deaths from 1 March 2016.
Complex eligibility conditions, difficulty of tracing back, and saving administrative costs are matters of administrative convenience, not an important public interest.

Even if finances and resource allocation are an important public interest, the restriction saves only a small amount from those who could not apply in time, which is not substantially linked to the survivors' interest it sacrifices.

who: Survivors of National Pension insured persons who died on or before 29 Feb 2016
Survivors who applied late for survivor's pension

raw.answer: A cigarette company, Japan Tobacco International's Taiwan unit, was fined NT$5 million for sponsoring an elderly-welfare project and publicizing its sponsorship, which authorities treated as tobacco promotion. It asked the Constitutional Court to review the tobacco control provisions and a ministry letter explaining them. The court held that the provisions and the letter do not violate the Constitution, and it declined to hear some other parts of the request.
raw.held: The definitions of tobacco advertising and sponsorship and the ban on promoting tobacco through events (Article 9, item 8) are not unconstitutionally vague, and the ban does not violate free speech or equality. The 2013 ministry letter (section 2) does not violate the legal reservation, non-retroactivity, reliance protection or proportionality principles.

points.text: The wording is not unconstitutionally vague. The terms can be understood from the text, purpose and the law as a whole, and people can foresee what is covered, which courts can review.

The ban limits tobacco companies' commercial speech, which gets less protection than other speech. But it does not ban all sponsorship by company name. Each case is judged on whether the sponsorship amounts to promoting tobacco.

The ban serves the important public interest of reducing tobacco use and protecting health. It has a substantial connection to that aim by stopping companies from using sponsorship as disguised advertising, so it does not violate free speech.

Treating tobacco companies differently is not unconstitutional. The aim is legitimate, the classification is not one needing strict review, and tobacco differs from alcohol or betel nut because secondhand smoke harms others.

The ministry letter only restates the scope of the existing provision and adds no new restriction. So it does not breach the legal reservation, non-retroactivity or reliance protection principles, and it is also proportionate.

Some parts of the request were not heard: the penalty provision, the tobacco control treaty, and another section of the letter, because they were not properly challengeable or not shown to be unconstitutional.

who: Organizations and people receiving sponsorship from tobacco companies
Health authorities enforcing the tobacco control law

raw.answer: A truck driver drove across a railway crossing just after the alarm sounded again, hit the barrier, and was fined NT$60,000, had his license revoked, was barred for life from getting a new one, and was ordered to attend a safety course. He argued these rules violated his constitutional rights. The court held the penalty rules do not violate the Constitution, but told the authorities to fix the lack of a minimum safe gap between alarms when trains pass in succession.
raw.held: The fine, license revocation, lifetime ban on re-applying (with the exceptions in Article 67-1) and mandatory safety course do not violate the proportionality principle or the protections of work, property and general freedom of action. The authorities must promptly review and improve how crossing alarms work when two or more trains pass one after another.

points.text: The rules limit general freedom of action, property (fines) and the right to work (license revocation for professional drivers), so they must meet the proportionality principle.
The purpose is to stop drivers running crossings, protecting the safety, lives, bodies and property of many people; this is a major public interest and a constitutional purpose.

The lifetime ban is harsh because it ignores how serious the violation was, but Article 67-1 lets drivers re-apply after 6, 8, 10 or 12 years, so it is not truly lifelong and is substantially related to the purpose.
The fine, and the limits on general freedom of action including the safety course, have a reasonable connection to the purpose and do not breach proportionality.

The state has a constitutional duty to build sound rules and safeguards for crossings, yet the existing rules set no minimum safe interval between one train's alarm ending and the next starting, sometimes only a few seconds.

Such short gaps can mislead drivers, especially of large vehicles, into entering the crossing and then being penalised, so the authorities must promptly improve this, for example with extended alarms.

who: Motor vehicle drivers, including professional drivers
Railway passengers and the public using crossings

raw.answer: When land or buildings go unregistered after an owner's death, they can eventually be sold at public auction by the national property agency. A lawful user of the property claimed a priority right to buy it, and the courts disagreed over whether a dispute about that right belongs in the ordinary (civil) courts or the administrative courts. The court ruled that it is a private-law dispute for the ordinary courts.
raw.held: A lawful user of unregistered inherited land or buildings who asserts a priority right to buy at a public sale by the national property agency (or its branches), and sues to confirm that right exists, is raising a private-law dispute. The lawsuit must be heard by the ordinary courts.

points.text: Taiwan uses two court systems. Where the law doesn't say which court hears a matter, the nature of the dispute decides: private-law disputes generally go to ordinary courts and public-law disputes to administrative courts.
The priority-purchase provision only says lawful users have the right and does not say which court hears disputes, so the court looked to the nature of the dispute.

Deciding whether someone is a lawful user means checking whether they have a legal basis for using the property, such as property rights, a lease or a loan. That is a question of private legal relationships.

The effect of the right is only to decide whether the claimant can replace the winning bidder as buyer in the sale contract. Both the requirements and the effect are governed by civil law and do not involve exercising public power.
So a lawsuit to confirm the priority right is a private-law dispute, and the ordinary courts hear it.

who: Lawful users of unregistered inherited land or buildings
The national property agency and its branches
Winning bidders at these public sales

raw.answer: Residents and a building management committee living next to a rezoned hospital site in Taichung argued the change harmed their rights, but the top administrative court dismissed their suit. Taiwan's Constitutional Court decided that people outside the boundary of an individual urban plan change must be allowed to bring an administrative lawsuit if the change harms their rights or legal interests. It said this adds to its earlier Interpretation No. 156.
raw.held: People outside the area of an individual urban plan change, whose rights or legal interests are harmed by it, must be allowed to sue in administrative court, and Interpretation No. 156 is supplemented accordingly. Whether harm actually occurred is for each case to decide.

points.text: The court accepted the petition because the final judgment relied on Interpretation No. 156 and left the petitioners without a remedy, which it found a proper reason to review.
Article 16 of the Constitution protects the right to sue, meaning a person whose rights or legal interests are harmed can ask a court for relief.
Under the principle that a right means a remedy, people harmed must get a chance to bring a case to court for fair and timely effective relief.

Interpretation No. 156's phrase 'people within a certain area' refers to people inside the changed area, but people outside it who are harmed must still be allowed to sue, so that interpretation is supplemented.
Whether rights or legal interests were actually harmed must be judged case by case.
The challenge to Article 19, paragraph 1 of the Urban Planning Act was not accepted because that provision does not affect the outcome of the judgment.

who: Residents living outside an urban plan change area
Building management committees next to changed areas

raw.answer: Two companies that make bottled products were ordered by Taiwan's environmental agency to pay recycling, clearance and disposal fees, including a heavier rate because their bottle caps or fittings used PVC plastic. They argued the fee rules were unconstitutional. The Constitutional Court found the challenged rules did not violate the Constitution.
raw.held: The court held that the challenged law and agency notices do not violate the principle that important matters need a legal basis, equal treatment, or proportionality, including the 100% higher rate for PVC fittings. It declined to hear a few parts of the petitions that did not concern provisions applied in the final judgments.

points.text: The fee is a money burden on people that limits property rights, so its purpose, payers, rate and use must be set by law. The law may let the central agency decide payers and rates within a clear authorization, because the subject is highly technical.

The law itself sets what counts as recyclable waste and who is responsible, and lets the agency fix the details. Making the maker of the bottled product, not the container maker, the fee payer was not arbitrary and fits the law's aim.
The law requires a review committee to examine rates and lists the factors to consider, so leaving the rate to the agency does not breach the legal basis or clear-authorization rules.

Charging by the combined weight of container and fittings can sometimes cost a company more, but that is an occasional result, not a systematic disadvantage. It applies to all cases alike and simplifies calculation and administration, a legitimate aim, so it does not breach equal protection.

The 100% higher rate for PVC fittings serves a proper aim of reducing a more environmentally harmful material. An earlier 30% increase had little effect, so the higher rate is reasonably related to the aim and proportionate.
Challenges to provisions not applied in the final judgments, and a request to supplement an earlier interpretation that was not applied, were not accepted.

raw.answer: Five landowners had successfully asked the court for Interpretation No. 742, which said people hit by certain city-planning reviews can seek administrative or court remedies. When they then reopened their case, the top administrative court rejected it because their appeal came far too late after the 1992 planning notice. The court decided that their reopening petition, filed within 30 days of the earlier interpretation's release, counts as filed within the legal appeal period.
raw.held: The petition for retrial that the petitioners filed within 30 days of the release of Interpretation No. 742 is treated as having been filed with the appeals authority within the legal time limit for an administrative appeal. Interpretation No. 742 is supplemented accordingly.

points.text: The court accepted the request because there was a justified doubt about how the appeal period should be counted under the earlier interpretation, in light of the constitutional protection of appeal and litigation rights.

Interpretations bind all agencies and the people, and also apply to the original case of the person who asked for them. Such petitioners may rely on a favorable interpretation from the day it is released.

Before Interpretation No. 742 there was no legal basis to appeal such reviews, so missing the deadline could not be blamed on the petitioners. It was also unrealistic to expect them to recognize the plan item as an administrative act open to review.
The petitioners' request led to the amendment of the Administrative Litigation Act and a new chapter on city-planning review, a real contribution to upholding the constitution.

Requiring an appeal within 30 days of the 1992 notice would impose too heavy a burden and would not adequately protect appeal and litigation rights, and the earlier interpretation had not addressed this. The supplement protects those rights and encourages people to seek constitutional review.

who: The five petitioners in the original case
Landowners affected by city-planning periodic reviews
Administrative agencies handling the appeal period

raw.answer: Several prisoners and a judge asked Taiwan's Constitutional Court whether prisoners may go to court when they dispute prison decisions, since the old rules only allowed an internal complaint to the supervising authority. The court held that, to the extent the rules bar court relief where a prison measure goes beyond what is necessary and unlawfully violates a constitutional right in a non-trivial way, they violate the constitutional right to sue. It set a 2-year deadline for revising the law and created a temporary route to court in the meantime.
raw.held: The two provisions are unconstitutional insofar as they deny prisoners court relief against prison measures that exceed what is necessary and unlawfully infringe constitutional rights in a non-minor way. Authorities must revise the law within 2 years, and until then a prisoner who is dissatisfied with the complaint decision may sue in the local district court's administrative division within 30 days.

points.text: The constitutional right to sue means people whose rights are harmed can seek court relief, and this cannot be denied just because of their status.

Prisons need to manage inmates to achieve the purpose of the sentence, so courts should give them considerable deference; trivial or non-rights-infringing measures go only through internal complaints. But when a measure exceeds what is necessary and unlawfully harms constitutional rights in a non-minor way, court access is allowed.
The complaint system is a legitimate design choice and lets prisons review themselves, but it cannot take away a prisoner's right to sue in court.

The old rules came from a time when prisoners were seen as in a special power relationship with no court access; an internal complaint is not equivalent to a court proceeding and cannot replace it. A ministry letter allowing referral to courts does not bind courts and the rules were never amended.
Barring court relief in those cases goes beyond what is necessary under Article 23 and conflicts with Article 16, so authorities must amend the law within 2 years.
Until the law is amended, prisoners may sue in the district court's administrative division after a complaint decision, within 30 days, under simplified procedures, possibly without oral hearing.

raw.answer: Police officers who passed the third-level special police exam before 2100 without a police-university background were always sent to the Police College for training, so they could not qualify for higher posts such as patrol inspector (巡官). The court held that, as applied in practice, this treated them unfairly and conflicted with the constitutional guarantee of equality. It ordered the Executive Yuan and the Examination Yuan to fix this within six months.
raw.held: Article 11, paragraph 2 of the Police Personnel Management Act, because it does not specify the training institution and lets the police agency send all such general-background examinees to the Police College, conflicts with the equality guarantee of Article 7 of the Constitution to that extent. The Executive Yuan, together with the Examination Yuan, must take suitable measures within six months to remove the unequal treatment the petitioners suffered.

points.text: The right to take exams and hold public office covers fair competition and training that completes the exam process to gain rank and job eligibility, and police posts count as public office. Those who pass the same exam must get qualifications consistent with equal treatment.
Because this right is a broad political right, unequal treatment of it gets stricter review: the aim must serve an important public interest and the means must be substantially related to that aim.

Passing the exam gives everyone the same rank, but graduates of the Police University or Police Officer School can be appointed to all posts at once, while others cannot be appointed as patrol inspector and similar posts without training at the university or school.

The rule looks open on its face, but in practice, before 2100, general-background examinees were always sent to the Police College and never got the university training, even after an appeals decision and a Control Yuan correction. This made the rule consistently favor university graduates and disadvantage them, so it counts as unequal treatment.

The rule does not name the training institution, so the police agency could send all such examinees to the Police College. This blocked their initial appointment as patrol inspector and made later promotion require extra selection and university training.

The agency's reasons did not justify this. Preserving the police education system does not require excluding them, training capacity is only an administrative cost and not an important public interest, and limited posts call for merit-based selection, not blanket assignment to the Police College.

who: Police third-level special exam passers from before 2100 without police-school background

raw.answer: A patient lost hearing after being treated with a drug and applied for drug-injury relief, but was refused because the harm was a common and foreseeable side effect. She asked the court to rule that the rule excluding such side effects (Article 13, item 9 of the Drug Injury Relief Act) was unconstitutional. The court held the rule is constitutional, while urging the authorities to review it and not to widen the exclusions too far.
raw.held: Article 13, item 9 of the Drug Injury Relief Act, which bars relief applications for common and foreseeable adverse drug reactions, does not violate the clarity principle or the proportionality principle, and does not conflict with the constitutional protection of the rights to life and health or the state's duty to value medical and health welfare.

points.text: The relief system exists to help people harmed by properly used, lawful drugs, and it fits the constitutional protection of life, health and medical welfare.

The terms 'common' and 'foreseeable' are vague concepts but not hard to understand in ordinary life, and 'adverse reaction' is defined in the Act. Patients can reasonably foresee them through doctors' disclosure, drug bag labels and package inserts.
The authority treats a reaction rate of 1% or more as 'common'. The review committee uses this standard, many cases exist, and courts can review the decision, so the rule meets the clarity principle.
Relief rules are social policy involving the allocation of state resources, so the legislature has wide discretion and the court applies a looser standard of review.

The exclusion has a legitimate purpose: keeping the relief fund financially balanced, using limited resources well, and avoiding drug makers refusing to supply effective drugs with common, foreseeable serious reactions.
Because such risks come with how drugs work and patients can reasonably foresee them, the exclusion helps the purpose, is not clearly unreasonable, and satisfies proportionality.

who: Patients harmed by drug side effects

raw.answer: Thirty-eight legislators challenged the 2018 amended law on military officers' and NCOs' service, which cut retirement benefits, including the preferential-deposit interest, for people already retired. They argued it breaks the ban on retroactive laws, the protection of reasonable reliance, proportionality, and rights such as property and equality. The court upheld nearly all the challenged rules, struck down the provision that stops retirement pay for those who take full-time teaching jobs at private universities, and told the government to fix the rule on inflation adjustments.
raw.held: Most challenged provisions (definitions, the new pay ceiling and floor, the phased cuts, higher contribution rates, return of deposit principal, settlement of monthly compensation, and fund top-up) were held not unconstitutional. Article 34(1)(3) violates equal protection and loses effect on the day of the ruling; Article 39(1) must be amended promptly to adjust pensions for consumer price increases; the request for a provisional order was rejected.

points.text: The cuts apply to benefit relationships that continue after the new law took effect and do not claw back money already paid, so they are not retroactive. Retirement benefits are also not deferred wages.

The cuts serve important public interests: narrowing unfair gaps between retirees with the same rank and service, easing the government's interest-subsidy burden, coping with an aging population, and keeping the retirement fund alive. Because the interest comes wholly from the government budget, the court reviewed them leniently.

Transition periods of 10 and 6 years, a minimum guarantee, and exemptions for the injured, disabled and those over 85 softened the impact, so the cuts were not excessive and respect reliance and proportionality.

Raising contribution rates, returning deposit principal in year 11, settling monthly compensation, and putting savings into the fund are reasonable. The higher rates only affect the future and help extend the fund's life.

The government's 'final payment guarantee' does not by itself make other reform measures unconstitutional. Under the shared-contribution system, the budget steps in only when other measures are not enough.

Stopping pension for those teaching full-time at private universities fails the strict equality test: its classification is too broad and too narrow compared with its goals. Separately, having no duty to adjust pensions for consumer prices is inconsistent with the reform's purpose.

who: Surviving family members receiving survivor pensions
